records.name_note: NC State is the only admissible source with a loadable dedicated page for this hybrid; the other sources could not be loaded or had no page. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list gives Everblooming Honeysuckle first and Goldflame Honeysuckle second, so common_name follows the first item. The given name, Goldflame Honeysuckle, is the second item, and NC State's Description prose refers to the plant as Goldflame honeysuckle. NC State writes the binomial in its heading with an ASCII x, normalised here to the multiplication sign, and its Description calls the taxon an artificial cross with a hybrid formula.
unknowns: Only plants.ces.ncsu.edu had a loadable dedicated page for Lonicera x heckrottii. RHS (guessed URLs returned 404), MoBot and plantfinder.mobot.org (connection refused from this sandbox), Clemson HGIC (HTTP 403), UF/IFAS and UMD (no hybrid page found), and the UGA field report (no page found) gave no usable page, so no second source corroborates any field.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: the NC State page for this hybrid carries no Poison block, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags and no toxicity statement. Berry warnings for other Lonicera were deliberately not applied. The page's Fruit field says the berries are red and Wildlife Value says berries are edible by birds, which is not a statement about cats or dogs.
is_edible is null: no admissible source addresses human eating of this hybrid; the bird-edible berry note is not an edibility claim.

is_houseplant false: the page treats it only as an in-ground shrub or vine (Plant Type lists Perennial, Shrub, Vine; Landscape Location lists Patio, Rock Wall, Vertical Spaces, Walkways; USDA zones 5a-8b) and does not address indoor culture.

mature_height_in 120-156 is NC State's Dimensions Height 10-13 ft, matched by its prose 'Goldflame honeysuckle can climb up to 13 feet, but it can be pruned to a 6-foot shrub, if desired.' The 6-foot figure is an optional pruned size, not the mature size. Width 3-6 ft is converted to 36-72 inches. The research record had left height null; landed at repair from the auditor's verified Dimensions text, as the catalog lands NC State's Dimensions height for Lonicera sempervirens and Lonicera japonica.
water_regime is null: NC State gives only the soil adjectives Moist and Occasionally Dry under Soil Drainage and no watering statement.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), which is open-ended, and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The prose says the plant is intolerant of alkaline soils, which conflicts with reading 8.0 as a ceiling, and no RHS pH field was available to check.

outdoor_sun_exposure maps NC State's Light values Full sun and Partial Shade to full_sun and part_shade. The hour figures inside those values are generic category definitions that NC State repeats on every plant page, not species-specific measurements, so direct_sun_hours_max is null. The prose says the flower display is poorer in shaded areas.

Hardiness: NC State lists USDA zones 5a to 8b, which is a growing-range limit and not a chill-damage onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null. NC State also notes the plant is listed as invasive in Illinois and has not been reported as invasive elsewhere.
No source gave light in foot-candles, humidity, temperature ranges, fertilizer guidance or watering intervals, so those fields are null.

records.name_note: Sources lean toward Rocky Mountain Juniper but are not uniform. UF/IFAS's dedicated page has a single "Common name(s)" line whose first item is Rocky mountain juniper (then Colorado redcedar). RHS's dedicated page is headed Juniperus scopulorum and shows Rocky Mountain juniper as its common name. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list is alphabetized and begins Colorado Red Cedar, but includes both Rocky Mountain Juniper and Rocky Mountain Red Cedar, and its description text calls the plant Rocky Mountain Juniper. NC State's "is often confused with" module names Juniperus virginiana. MoBot could not be loaded, so it was not used.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible source names cats or dogs. RHS (Potentially harmful field, not scoped to any animal): "Harmful if eaten/skin allergen. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling". NC State carries no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tag on this page; its Tags include "#contact dermatitis". NC State Plant Type: Tree. NC State's ethnobotany note says Native Americans used the juniper berries for food and decorations, which conflicts with RHS's "harmful if eaten", so edibility is left unresolved.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org / plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be loaded from the sandbox (ConnectError), so no MoBot citation is used. Clemson HGIC's juniper factsheet returned 403 and is a multi-species page anyway.

toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity evidence (RHS 'Harmful if eaten/skin allergen') names no animal, and NC State has no Poison block or cat/dog tag on this page (only a '#contact dermatitis' tag).
is_edible left null: NC State's Uses (Ethnobotany) says Native Americans used the juniper berries for food, while RHS says harmful if eaten; sources disagree, so no edibility claim is made.
outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field also lists Partial Shade (2-6 hours), but UF/IFAS (full sun) and RHS (Position Full sun) exclude it, so only full_sun is recorded.

soil_drainage moderate: NC State's Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage + Moist + Occasionally Dry, its text says moist well-drained soils (and does especially well in dry sandy soil, cannot tolerate wet soils), and RHS says well-drained or moist but well-drained. This is not fast because the sources describe moist but well-drained soil rather than sharp drainage only. UF says it is difficult to grow in the south due to disease problems and, if you try it, to provide excellent drainage and keep the foliage dry.
soil_ph left null: RHS lists neutral, alkaline or acid and UF lists acidic and alkaline soils, so no floor or ceiling is supported.
water_regime, water_dry_down_target and watering day-intervals left null: no source gives a watering statement for this in-ground tree; moisture words are soil adjectives or tolerance traits.
humidity_need left null: NC State's 'cannot tolerate high humidity' is an outdoor tolerance aside, not a care target.
chill_damage_f, temperature, light_fc, fertilizer fields left null: no admissible source states them. NC State and UF zone ranges (NC 3a-7b, UF 4A-9A) are hardiness ranges, not damage onset.

Size: NC State Dimensions height 30-40 ft (360-480 in) and width 3-15 ft (36-180 in) are used; NC State's description and UF also say 30 to 40 feet tall, and UF gives spread 10 to 15 feet. RHS's description says the tree reaches a height of 15m (about 591 in); its size fields give Max Height 'Higher than 12 metres' and Max Spread 4-8 metres (about 157-315 in). RHS's height and spread run larger than the US sources, and the spread figures disagree across sources.

Cedar-apple rust: NC State says Phomopsis twig blight may occur as well as Cedar-apple rust and other rust diseases. UF says the three rust diseases seen most often are cedar-apple, hawthorn and quince rust, that cedar-apple is the most common, and that spores formed in the horns infect the alternate host, where the diseases are more serious than on juniper. UF does not name the alternate host species.

attracts_pollinators true rests on NC State's structured Attracts field (Butterflies, Songbirds); no source states the tree is bee- or butterfly-pollinated, and NC State says pollen is dispersed by wind.

NC State says the species cannot tolerate wet soils, high humidity, nor high night temperatures; it says the tree could possibly be attempted in the mountains of North Carolina but that it may be best to consider the closely related Eastern Red Cedar, which is better able to handle North Carolina's hot, humid weather. UF says it is difficult to grow in the south due to disease problems.

records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) list renders Bearberry Cotoneaster first, followed by Cotoneaster humifusa and Cotoneaster humifusus as separate entries; RHS lists the same two names as synonyms. The common name 'bearberry' is also used for Arctostaphylos uva-ursi (NC State's page for that species lists Bearberry first), so this record is matched on the binomial, not the common name.
records.toxicity_detail: No admissible page for this exact taxon names cats or dogs, and neither carries a cyanogenic-compound statement. NC State's Description says "Ingested fruits may cause mild stomach upset." with no animal or person named; the page has no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags. RHS's Potentially harmful block (fruit only, no poison-part list or symptom list given) reads: "Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and "Pets: Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". RHS's 'Pets' wording names no animal, so toxic_to_pets is left null.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity wording found is NC State's unscoped 'Ingested fruits may cause mild stomach upset.' and RHS's 'Pets:' line, which names no cat or dog. No cyanogenic-compound statement appears on either dedicated page.

MoBot and Clemson/UF/PSU/UMD/UGA: no dedicated species page for Cotoneaster dammeri could be loaded or confirmed (MoBot's page only surfaced as the 'Coral Beauty' cultivar; plantfinder/missouribotanicalgarden hosts failed to connect; Clemson returned 403), so only NC State and RHS are used.

Fire blight susceptibility as sourced: NC State says 'Scale and fireblight can also affect this plant.' and lists Fire Blight among common disease problems; RHS says 'May be susceptible to fire blight and honey fungus'.

Size sources differ: NC State gives height 1 ft (12 in) and width 4-6 ft (48-72 in); RHS gives Max Height 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in) and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59-98 in). NC State used as anchor.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) with open-ended outer bands, and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral.
water_regime null: sources give only drought tolerance and 'Occasional watering will give you a better fruit production', not a watering regime.

is_edible null: NC State says bears, birds and animals eat the berries, and RHS says the fruit is 'not to be eaten'; no source states the plant is grown or used for food or that it is poisonous to eat.

is_houseplant false: neither source addresses indoor culture; NC State presents an outdoor ground cover shrub (Plant Type Ground Cover, Shrub; USDA zones 5a-8b) whose Landscape Location list includes Container alongside outdoor locations but no Houseplants value.
soil_base garden_bed is chosen from in-ground culture wording (rock gardens, low banks) rather than an explicit potting-mix statement.
RHS: Hardiness rating H6 ('hardy in all of UK and northern Europe (-20 to -15)') is a survival rating, not a damage-onset temperature, so chill_damage_f is null.

records.name_note: NC State, the only admissible source reached with a dedicated page for this hybrid, heads the page with an ASCII x (Magnolia x loebneri), normalised here to the multiplication sign; its Common Name(s) list carries the single entry Loebner Magnolia, and its Previously known as field lists Magnolia kobus var. loebneri. No admissible source disagrees on the common name or on hybrid status.
unknowns: Only NC State's dedicated Magnolia x loebneri page could be read. The Missouri Botanical Garden page (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid 249468) failed to load from this machine (certificate and connection errors), so it is not cited. RHS lists only cultivar pages for this hybrid, which do not count. Clemson's Magnolia factsheet is genus-level, so it was not used.

No admissible source read states toxicity to cats or dogs for this hybrid, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. ASPCA's Magnolia grandiflora listing is not extended to this hybrid. NC State's page carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags.
is_edible is null because NC State does not address eating the plant.
is_houseplant false: no source frames it as an indoor plant. NC State presents a deciduous landscape tree or large shrub (Plant Type Shrub, Tree; Landscape Location Lawn, Patio; USDA zones 5a-9b).
water_regime is null: NC State gives only soil adjectives (Moist, Good Drainage) and no watering statement. The page also says the plant is intolerant of extremely wet or dry soil.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State shows Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) bands, which are open-ended or bands rather than a stated range. The prose says slightly acidic with no numbers, and there is no RHS pH field to cross-check a ceiling.

direct_sun_hours_max is null: the page's species prose says full sun or partial shade without stating hours. The 2-6 hour figure inside NC State's Partial Shade value is a generic category definition it repeats on every plant page, so it was not used. Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade.
Chill damage onset is not stated. NC State says late spring frosts can damage flower buds, and says the plant is rated zones 5a-9b. Neither is an onset temperature.

Mature size 8-30 ft (96-360 in) for both height and width is the Dimensions block on NC State's own Magnolia x loebneri page, matched by its prose 'It is a smaller magnolia, 8 to 30 feet tall, and equally as wide'. Cultivar sizes listed on the page were not used.
Humidity, temperature ranges, fertilizing and indoor light are all null: they were not addressed by an admissible dedicated-page source.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated page and RHS's dedicated page both lead with the common name lily magnolia. RHS also lists the other common names mu-lan, purple-flowered magnolia and woody orchid. NC State lists Magnolia quinquepeta and Yulania liliiflora under "Previously known as".
unknowns: Toxicity: neither NC State's nor RHS's Magnolia liliiflora page carries any poison or pet-toxicity information, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null and nothing was borrowed from M. grandiflora.

is_edible is null: the NC State page only says the flowers and buds have been used medicinally and neither page addresses eating. is_houseplant false: both pages treat it as an outdoor shrub or small tree (NC State Plant Type Perennial, Shrub, Tree; Landscape Location Container, Patio; USDA zones 5a-8b) and neither addresses indoor culture.
attracts_pollinators is null: NC State's page carries no Attracts field and RHS's page carries no pollinator tag.

Only two admissible pages for this exact taxon were found (NC State and RHS). No dedicated Magnolia liliiflora page was found on MoBot (kempercode scan of the Magnolia entries a881-a885 and c117-c119 turned up other magnolias only, and site search returned nothing), Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA searches. MoBot's host also serves an incomplete certificate chain, so its pages could only be read with verification off.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists full sun (6 or more hours) and partial shade (2-6 hours of direct sun); RHS Position lists Full sun and Partial shade. Both are mapped to full_sun and part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null because no species prose gives an hour figure.

Mature size: NC State's Dimensions block (8-12 ft = 96-144 in) is the anchor. RHS lists Max Height and Max Spread of 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in) at 10-20 years to maturity, which is slightly larger; NC State's figures were used.

soil_ph_max 8.0 comes from the closed top of NC State's Neutral (6.0-8.0) band; RHS pH field lists only Acid or Neutral (no alkaline), so the ceiling stands. NC State's Acid (<6.0) band is open-ended so soil_ph_min is null. NC State's prose says neutral to slightly acidic, which is tighter than that structured ceiling.

water_regime is null: NC State's prose says medium moisture and well-drained soils and its Soil Drainage tags are Good Drainage and Moist, and RHS Moisture says moist but well-drained or well-drained; none of these is a watering statement for a keep_moist or dry-between regime. NC State's Drought resistance tag is a trait, not a watering instruction. Day-interval and dry-down fields are null for an in-ground shrub.

chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, temperature, humidity, light_fc and fertilizer fields are null: no admissible page states them. NC State's USDA zones 5a-8b and RHS's H6 are hardiness ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.

records.name_note: Sources differ slightly in lead name. RHS's dedicated page shows 'laurustinus' as the common name under its Viburnum tinus heading (and lists 'common laurustinus, tinus' as other common names); NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list reads Laurustine, Laurustinus Viburnum, with Laurustine first. 'Laurustinus' is used because RHS leads with it and it appears in NC State's list as 'Laurustinus Viburnum'.
records.toxicity_detail: RHS 'Potentially harmful' block (no heading severity rating, symptom list or poison-part list given): 'Fruit are ornamental - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling.' The RHS Pets line reads 'Pets: Fruit are ornamental; not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers', which names no animal (no cat or dog), so toxic_to_pets is left null. The NC State page carries no toxicity block. The RHS statement is fruit-scoped.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden (plantfinder.mobot.org) page for V. tinus (taxonid 279005) could not be fetched (connection error from the sandbox, TLS verification failure via WebFetch), so no MoBot evidence was used; Clemson HGIC and UF/IFAS have only a genus-level Viburnum factsheet or no V. tinus page, so were not used.

toxic_to_pets left null: the only toxicity evidence (RHS) is fruit-scoped and its Pets line names no animal. toxicity_detail has no symptom list, poison-part list or severity rating because none is given.
is_edible left null: RHS says the fruit are ornamental and 'not to be eaten' but does not state the plant is poisonous or inedible; NC State does not address eating.
is_houseplant false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture; NC State presents an outdoor shrub (Plant Type Perennial, Shrub; Landscape Location Coastal; USDA zones 8a-10b).

outdoor_sun_exposure: RHS Position also lists full shade, but NC State's structured Light field gives only full sun and partial shade, so full_shade is left out. NC State 'Partial Shade' mapped to part_shade.
soil_ph_min/max null: RHS lists pH 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no bounds can be set.

water_regime null: the only moisture statements are RHS's soil-moisture field and cultivation soil description, not a watering instruction; NC State's page gives Good Drainage only, with no moisture tag. NC State also lists drought as a resistance trait, which is not a watering statement.

soil_drainage moderate rests on RHS's species-specific cultivation sentence 'moist but well-drained' (its text differs from the V. dentatum RHS page); NC State's bare Good Drainage alone would be ambiguous.
soil_base null: both sources describe in-ground landscape culture, not a container mix.

Size from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 6-12 ft, Width 6-10 ft, converted to inches). RHS gives a larger Max Height of 2.5-4 metres and Max Spread of 2.5-4 metres (about 98-157 in) at a Time to Maturity of 10–20 years; that disagreement is not used.
chill_damage_f null: RHS hardiness H4 and NC State USDA zones 8a-10b are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures.
Temperature, humidity, light footcandle, fertilizer and watering-interval fields have no admissible-source support.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name: NC State's Common Name(s) list (alphabetized) begins Chinese Holly, RHS gives holly olive beneath the binomial in its profile heading and lists Chinese holly and false holly as other common names, and UF/IFAS lists false holly first. False Holly was chosen because it is the first item of the UF/IFAS dedicated page's list and the name NC State's own description prose uses. Holly Osmanthus appears in the NC State and UF/IFAS lists but is not first on either. This is not an Ilex: NC State says its leaves are opposite whereas true holly leaves are alternate.
unknowns: Toxicity: no admissible dedicated page for this species states any toxicity or pet safety (NC State shows no Poison block or Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags; RHS and UF/IFAS are silent), so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null. Ilex toxicity was not borrowed.
is_edible and attracts_pollinators are null: no admissible source addresses eating, and neither NC State (no Attracts field) nor RHS (no pollinator tag) names pollinators.
MoBot Plant Finder page (taxonid=283003) could not be fetched here (ConnectError on all hosts), so no MoBot content was used; Clemson HGIC has only a genus-level Tea Olive page, which was not used.

Mature size: NC State gives Height 8-20 ft and Width 7-20 ft (96-240 and 84-240 in), used as the anchor. UF/IFAS gives Height 8 to 15 feet and Spread 10 to 18 feet; RHS gives Max Height and Max Spread 4-8 metres (157-315 in) over 10-20 years. The published ranges differ and the NC State range was chosen.

Soil pH: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) and RHS lists acid, alkaline or neutral, so no floor or ceiling is set. NC State's description prose says it prefers acidic soil and tolerates alkaline soil.

water_regime is null: NC State's Moist is a soil-drainage tag, RHS's Moisture field is a soil adjective, and UF/IFAS only states drought tolerance once established, which is a tolerance trait. No watering statement was found. Related UF/IFAS warning: mushroom root rot is troublesome when the soil is kept too wet. Dry-down and interval fields are left null for an in-ground shrub.
soil_drainage moderate is read from NC State's Good Drainage plus Moist pair and RHS's well-drained or moist but well-drained; UF/IFAS's root-rot warning agrees.

Sun: NC State (Full sun and Partial Shade tags), RHS (Full sun, Partial shade) and UF/IFAS (part shade/part sun) agree on this set; UF/IFAS also says grown in sun or shade, which was not used to add full_shade.

Temperature, humidity, light (fc), chill damage and fertilizing: no admissible source states these for this species; hardiness zone 7-9 (NC State, UF/IFAS) and RHS H5 are survival ratings, not damage-onset temperatures. is_houseplant false: no source frames it as a houseplant; NC State presents an outdoor shrub or tree (Plant Type Perennial, Shrub, Tree; Landscape Location Patio, Woodland; USDA zones 7a-9b) and UF/IFAS a hedge, foundation plant or screen.

records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the lead common name. NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list runs Anemone Clematis, Himalayan Clematis, Mountain Clematis, in that order, though its Description opens with 'Mountain clematis'. RHS's dedicated page shows Himalayan clematis as its common name under the Clematis montana heading, and its Other common names field lists mountain clematis, without Anemone Clematis. Anemone Clematis was chosen because it leads NC State's Common Name(s) list.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block, under its human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' heading: Poison Severity: High. Poison Symptoms: "Clematis can cause severe mouth pain and ulcers if eaten. Toxic to dogs, cats, horses. Clinical signs are salivation, vomiting, diarrhea. In humans, symptoms may include dizziness, confusion, fainting, and convulsions. Fatalities are rare, due to the rapid and intense bitter taste and mouth irritation from eating. Gastric lavage is recommended and anti-inflammatory to soothe irritated tissue. Contact dermatitis results in skin redness and burning sensation for some people, gardening gloves are recommended." Poison Toxic Principle: protoanemonin. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Leaves, Sap/Juice. Separately, NC State's Problems field lists Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses, and its Plant Type field lists Perennial, Poisonous, Vine. toxic_to_pets is true on the Poison Symptoms text 'Toxic to dogs, cats, horses.' and the cat- and dog-scoped Problems values; the High severity rating is the human-scoped block's. RHS separately carries a handling warning: "Skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and "Pets (rabbits): Harmful if eaten." (rabbit-scoped only; not used for toxic_to_pets). No admissible source states a toxic dose.
unknowns: mature_height_in 192-480 is NC State's Dimensions Height 16-40 ft; its prose says 'Depending upon the support structure, it can climb 16 to 40 feet high and spread 8 to 15 feet wide.' RHS's Max Height field reads 8-12 metres (about 315-472 in), broadly consistent. The research record had left height null; landed at repair, as the catalog lands climbing heights for Clematis terniflora and Campsis radicans.
Spread uses NC State Dimensions Width 8-15 ft (96-180 in); RHS Max Spread 2.5-4 metres (98.4-157.5 in) is broadly consistent.

Pruning and bloom habit (not schema fields): NC State says it blooms on previous season's growth, so prune after flowering (Type 1); RHS says Pruning (Clematis) Group 1, flowers on previous season's growth. Flowers late spring to early summer per NC State.
toxic_to_pets rests on NC State only (Toxic to dogs, cats, horses; Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags). RHS's pet warning names rabbits only. ASPCA not an admissible source.

water_regime left null: no admissible source states a watering instruction for this species. NC State's 'Mulch the plant to help keep the roots cool and moist' and RHS's Moisture 'Moist but well-drained' are soil/mulch statements, not watering guidance. The RHS Cultivation sentence on moisture-retentive soil may be genus boilerplate and was not used.

soil_ph_max left null: NC State lists both Alkaline (>8.0), an open-ended band, and Neutral (6.0-8.0), and RHS lists pH Alkaline or Neutral, so no ceiling is supported. soil_ph_min 6.0 is the lower bound of NC State's Neutral band; no Acid band is listed.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours); RHS lists Full sun, Partial shade. Partial Shade mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max left null because the hour figures inside NC State's Light values are generic category definitions it repeats on every plant page, not species-specific measurements.

soil_base garden_bed reflects in-ground culture only (NC State describes well-drained soil high in organic matter); it is not a houseplant mix. is_houseplant false: both sources frame it as an outdoor landscape vine (NC State's Landscape Location Patio, Vertical Spaces, Walkways; USDA zones 6a-9b) and neither addresses indoor culture.
is_edible false: NC State says it is poisonous (severe mouth pain and ulcers if eaten); no source describes any edible use. RHS only gives a rabbit-scoped harmful-if-eaten note.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer, chill damage and watering-interval fields are null: no admissible source supports them. Hardiness zones (NC State 6a-9b, RHS H5) are not damage-onset temperatures.

Missouri Botanical Garden has only a Clematis montana f. grandiflora page, not the species, so it was excluded. Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, Maryland and UGA pages for this exact species were not located.
NC State's Resistance To Challenges field lists Black Walnut, Deer and Rabbits; not schema fields.

citations.claim: toxicity_detail: NC State's full Poison block, rendered under the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' heading (Poison Severity High, Causes Contact Dermatitis Yes)
citations.source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Clematis montana
citations.quote:
Poison Severity:
High
Poison Symptoms:
Clematis can cause severe mouth pain and ulcers if eaten. Toxic to dogs, cats, horses. Clinical signs are salivation, vomiting, diarrhea. In humans, symptoms may include dizziness, confusion, fainting, and convulsions. Fatalities are rare, due to the rapid and intense bitter taste and mouth irritation from eating. Gastric lavage is recommended and anti-inflammatory to soothe irritated tissue. Contact dermatitis results in skin redness and burning sensation for some people, gardening gloves are recommended.
Poison Toxic Principle:
protoanemonin
Causes Contact Dermatitis:
Yes
Poison Part:
Leaves
Sap/Juice
